title: Dancing in the street
hook: Mira sang and danced with wandering devotees, to her family's shame
tomorrow: if songs carry Mira's name, who actually wrote them?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poison cup. Tradition says Mira drank what the palace sent her, and it turned to nectar. Today, what she did next, where everyone could see.
screen: `POISON TURNED TO NECTAR.` → `WHERE EVERYONE COULD SEE.`

segments.voice: Someone posts a video of their grandmother dancing at a wedding, and the comments split: iconic, or embarrassing. Mira's in-laws chose embarrassing. The stories put her in a temple courtyard, bells tied around her ankles, singing to Krishna among wandering holy men, the people a princess of the royal house of Mewar was never supposed to sit with. Word reaches the palace, and the whispering starts in every room. Their own daughter-in-law, dancing where anyone at all can watch.
screen: `ICONIC, OR EMBARRASSING?` → `BELLS ON HER ANKLES.` → `AMONG THE WANDERING HOLY MEN.` → `WORD REACHES THE PALACE.`

segments.voice: The palace says stop. Her songs answer. One line sung under her name, in her own Rajasthani, goes pag ghunghru bandh Mira nachi re: Mira tied bells on her feet and danced. In other songs she says she has let go of the family's honor and the world's talk, because her lord is Giridhar Gopal, Krishna, the cowherd who lifted a mountain. Her family saw a scandal: a royal woman, out in a crowd of wanderers and street singers. Mira saw a love that couldn't stay behind a curtain, any more than a bride could hide her joy on her wedding day. That love has a name. Mira belongs to bhakti, the Hindu path of loving devotion to God. Bhakti says love for God isn't only for priests, or for the temple's inner room. It is sung out loud, in your own language, together, and sometimes danced. You can hear that in the kirtan and bhajans sung in Hindu temples and living rooms, with clapping, drums and voices answering each other, and Mira's songs are still danced to. The stories add one more line she crossed. Some tellings give her a teacher, the poet-saint Raidas, a leatherworker by caste, someone her royal family would have looked down on. Scholars can't confirm that meeting; the songs and stories keep it. Bhakti's point isn't to cause a scene. It is that a love this real doesn't hide.
screen: `PAG GHUNGHRU BANDH MIRA NACHI RE.` · `HER LORD: GIRIDHAR GOPAL.` · `BHAKTI: LOVE OF GOD, OUT LOUD.` · `A TEACHER FROM BELOW HER CASTE.` · then, large: `SHE DANCED.`

segments.voice: Think of one joy you keep quiet: a song you only sing alone, something you love and shrug off when anyone asks. For two minutes, let it be as big as it really is. Hum it, or let your feet keep time, and don't apologize to anyone.
Dancing in the street: Mira's devotion to Krishna, sung and danced in public while her royal family called it shame. In bhakti, love for God goes out loud.
Your line: she danced. The palace called it shame, and the songs called it love. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Devotees sing Mira's bhajans in temples and homes, often in a group with clapping, drums and harmonium, and sometimes dance; kirtan is sung as call and response.

fork.setup: you're at a friend's family puja. the aunties start a bhajan, and people begin clapping and swaying. you know none of the words. what fits what Mira's story teaches?
options: clap along if you're welcome; in bhakti the shared singing is the devotion itself.
stay still and silent; real devotion is private and shouldn't be watched.

fork.reveal: in bhakti, singing together is the worship, not a warm-up. Mira's songs went out loud, among ordinary devotees.
